full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman J : In this Rule Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181 /Aa:/ Mongla/12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 from the petitioner as customs duties should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect; and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. At the time of issuance of the Rule, further operation of the impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181/ Aa:/Mongla /12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) was stayed by this Court for a prescribed period.

3. Facts, necessary for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that the petitioner is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994. In course of business it decided to set up an ultra-modern condensate refinery plant under the name and style "Petromax Refinery Ltd" in order to refining, bottling, drumming, transporting, selling, and marketing of all sorts of edible oil including petroleum. The petitioner company duly registered its name with the VAT authority under the Value Added Tax (VAT) Act, 1991 (in short, the Act of 1991) for the purpose of payment of VAT and since its registration it has been paying VAT regularly. It has also been registered with the Board of Investment (in short, BOI) on 19-8-2009 having registration No. L-170309080361-1. However, the Bol by its letter dated 19-8-2009 permitted the petitioner to import machinery, equipment, components and materials to set up a complete automatic condensate refinery plant.

4. After obtaining permission from the government and completing all necessary formalities as required under the law, the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit being No. 086213020075 dated 18-4-2013 to import condensate (Crude oil) from Malaysia under HS Code No. 7209.00.00. After arrival of the goods at Mongla Port, Khulna, it, however, collected shipping documents from its respective bank and submitted Bill of Entry being No. C-4338 dated 29-5-2013 enclosing those documents through its Clearing and Forwarding (C&F) agent for assessing and releasing the same. After submission of Bill of Entry, the imported goods were inspected by the concerned Customs authority and found that the goods were in accordance with declaration. Pursuant thereto the respondent Customs authority made assessment of the goods on 3-6-2013 and upon payment of all customs duty, taxes and other charges those were released in favour of the petitioner and accordingly, it took delivery of the same.

5. Suddenly, the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs issued the impugned demand notice on 29-10-2013 upon the petitioner demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 with request to deposit the said amount within 10 (ten) days, failing which action would be taken under section 202 of the Customs Act, 1969 (in short, the Act of 1969).

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid demand notice the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule Nisi with interim order of stay.

7. The respondent No.2, the Commissioner of Customs entered appearance by filing affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that after 4 (four) months from the date of release of the goods an audit was conducted by the Customs authority and it was found that the previous assessment was made by the Customs authority on the basis of the declaration of the petitioner in its Bill of Entry without following the provision of law.

8. It has been stated further that the invoice value of the petitioner's imported goods was higher than its tariff value and the petitioner was liable to pay customs duty and taxes on the basis of invoice value as per provision of section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 and that the amount of public money was undisputed and was demanded on the basis of the petitioner's invoice value.

9. Considering the context of the case the Rule is liable to be discharged.

10. Countering, the aforesaid assertion of the respondent No. 2, the petitioner submitted affidavit-in-reply on 6-11-2008 contending, inter alia, that the petitioner has executed an agreement with Bangladesh Petroliam Corporation on 17-9-2012 to supply petroleum product and the tariff value of the goods has been fixed by the Government by Gazette notification. Moreover, the petitioner was not allowed to supply its imported goods to any other authority other than Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation.

11. It has been stated that the Government exercising the power as conferred under section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 promulgated SRO No. 159-Ain/2012/2387/Customs dated 7-6-2012 fixing the tariff value of different types of goods under different HS Codes and therein, the Government also fixed the unit of specified goods. Wherefrom it is apparent that the tariff value of the petitioner's imported goods was fixed at the rate of USD $ 32 per barrel (in short, BBL).

12. It has been stated further that the Second Secretary (Customs, Policy and Budget), National Board of Revenue passed an order on 25-8-2014 under Nothi No. ০৮.০১.০০০০.৫৩.০৩.০০৯.১৪/৫৫৩(১) informing all the concerned stating, inter alia, that the Government of Bangladesh, after special consideration and for the general interest of the people has taken a decision to exempt any customs duty and VAT on the additional value e. declared invoice value and the tariff value for all petroleum and petroleum-related goods as per section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 and that the aforesaid decision shall have retrospective effect covering from 9th June, 2005. Said decision is still pending for publication in the Gazette notification.

13. In this regard it has been stated that in the year 2014, the petitioner imported similar kinds of goods and those were assessed on the basis of tariff value and were accordingly released by furnishing bank guarantees for the differential amount. But, the Customs authority did not make final assessment within the prescribed period in law. The petitioner in the year 2018, however, filed writ petition No. 7329 of 2018 before this Hon'ble Court seeking direction upon the respondent Customs authority to return the bank guarantee which was furnished by the petitioner at the time of releasing the goods treating the provisional assessment as final as per section 81(2) of the Act, 1969. Upon hearing of the said writ petition, this Hon'ble Court vide order dated 28-5-2018 issued a Rule Nisi with direction upon the Customs authority to maintain status-quo in respect of encashment of the bank guarantees. Against the said interim order, the National Board of Revenue filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2616 of 2018 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Said Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was ultimately dismissed on 12-7-2018. The Rule of the said writ petition is still pending for hearing and disposal.

14. Conversely, the respondent No. 2 submitted supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-opposition on 10-12-2018 con-tending, inter alia, that pursuant to letter dated 25-8-2015 issued by the Second Secretary, National Board of Revenue (Annexure-Y to the Affidavit-in-reply), a summary was placed before the Hon'ble Minister, Ministry of Finance for approval and the same was ultimately approved. However, prior to publication of the notification in the official Gazette, it was sent to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for vetting.

Accordingly, said Ministry after vetting furnished an opinion that there was no scope to exempt the said taxes and duties as per the law and further made opinion to take legal steps for recovery of the government revenue in accordance with law.

15. Ms. Shamima Binte Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner by placing the writ petition and the relevant materials on record at the very outset submits that section 32(3) of the Act, 1969 provides the provision for realization of short levied taxes, duties and other charges by reasons of inadvertence, error or misconstruction through issuing show cause notice but, the impugned demand was made for short levied taxes and duties without issuing any show cause notice in violation of section 32(3) of the said Act. She further goes to submit that without amending the assessment under section 83A of the Act, 1969, the respondents have no authority to re-open the assessment file under which the goods had already been assessed and released; consequently, the impugned demand is absolutely illegal and liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority. She again goes to argue that the petitioner being a citizen of Bangladesh has fundamental right guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution to be treated equally and its right to be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law, as, has also been guaranteed under Article 31 of the Constitution. But, the Customs authority without following the provision of law issued the impugned notice upon the petitioner demanding the additional duty and taxes. Accordingly, she finally canvasses that issuance of the impugned notice being illegal and without jurisdiction is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and hence, of no legal effect.

16. In order to substantiate her contention the learned Advocate has relied upon the decisions of the case of SK Akijuddin Ltd. Vs National Board of Revenue reported in 16 BLC 692, the case of Md Musa Bhuiyan vs The Commissioner of Customs, Dhaka reported in 23 BLC 663, and an unreported decision of the case of Jalal Uddin vs National Board of Revenue, in Writ Petition No 1144 of 2006 (we are the parties of the said judgment).

17. Per Contra, Mr Shamsuddoha Talukder, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2 referring to section 25(3) of the Act submits that said provision of law provides that when the declared value of any imported goods is higher than its tariff value the customs duties and taxes shall be chargeable on the basis of its declared value and the respondent Customs authority issued the impugned notice demanding the actual customs duty and taxes following the said provision of law. He further goes to submit that the impugned demand has been made on the basis of admitted declared invoice value of the petitioner and giving opportunity of time to pay the demand amount, as such there is no requirement to issue any show cause notice for realization of the admitted government revenue. Hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

18. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No. 2, have perused the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition and the affidavit-in-reply with relevant materials on record so have been appended thereto and relevant provisions of law.

19. As it appears that the petitioner opened a Letter of Credit bearing No. 086213020075 dated 18-4-2013 for US $ 75,00,000 to import 10,000 Metric Ton condensate (Crude oil) under HS Code No. 2709.00.00 from Malaysia (Annexure-B). Accordingly, the supplier made part shipment of the goods i.e 5,562.185 Metric Ton out of 10,000 Metric Ton equivalent to 46308.00 BBL at the rate of US $ 112.643 per BBL, total invoice value of goods US$ 52,16,272.04 (as evidenced vide Annexure-C). After arrival of the goods at Mongla port, lamina, the petitioner, however, collected its shipping documents from its bank and generated Bill of Entry through its C&F agent and submitted the same to the Customs authority vide Entry No. C-4338 dated 29-5-2013 as per section 79 of the Act 1969 for assessment and releasing the goods (Annexure-D).

20. For the purpose of the assessment, the value of imported crude oil under HS Code No. 2709.00.00 was fixed by the government at the rate of US$ 32.00 per barrel (BBL) by publishing notification in the official Gazette vide SRO No 159-Ain/2012/12387 Customs dated 7-6-2013 (Annexure-X to the affidavit-in-reply) under section 25(3) of the Act. For ready reference sections 25(3) and 79 are quoted below:-"Section 25(3):, Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix, for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values (or minimum values) for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem: Provided that any imported or exported goods, the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section, shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value.

(4)

(5)

(6)

"Section 79:—Entry for home-consumption or ware housing: (1) The owner of any imported goods shall make entry of such goods for home-consumption or warehousing or for any other approved purpose by delivering to the appropriate officer a bill of entry thereof in such form and manner and containing such particulars as the Board may direct: Provided that, if the owner makes and subscribes a declaration before the appropriate officer to the effect that he is unable, for want of (such information as is essential for submitting a bill of entry), then the said officer shall permit him, previous to the entry thereof, to examine the goods in the presence of an officer of customs or to deposit such goods in a public warehouse appointed under section 12 without warehousing the same, pending the production of such information."

21. Vide section 25(3) of the Act the government for the purpose of levying customs duties and taxes may fix tariff or minimum values for any imported or exported goods as chargeable with customs duty advalorem. But, when the declared value of any imported or exported goods is higher than its tariff value the Customs duty and taxes shall be chargeable on the basis of declared value.

22. Section 79 of the Customs Act provides that the owner of any imported goods within specified period as provided under this section shall make entry of such goods or entry in electronic form by delivery to the appropriate office a Bill of Entry duly signed by him or his authorized agent thereof in such form and manner containing such particulars, as the Board may direct or the such information and documents as the Commissioner of Customs may specified.

23. Following section 79 of the Act, the petitioner had generated its Bill of Entry (Annexure-D) mentioning tarrif value of the goods in Box No. 22 US$ 1332592.00 (as per tariff value per BBL US $ 32) and accordingly, took delivery of the goods upon payment of customs duty and taxes being assessed by the Customs authority on the said tariff value. But, it appears from the petitioner's commercial Invoice (Annexure-C) that the actual transaction invoice value of the goods was US$ 52,16,272.04. (unit price 112.643/BBL) which was the actual value of the imported goods and that the said value was not denied by the petitioner before the respondent Customs authority or before this Court. Moreover, the invoice value of the goods i.e. US$ 52,16,272.04 is higher than its tariff/minimum value US$ 13,32,592.00. Accordingly, in view of section 25(3) of the Act when the declared value of any imported or exported goods is higher than its tariff value, the customs duties shall be chargeable on the basis of its declared value. Under the above legal position Cue petitioner was liable to pay customs duty and taxes chargeable on its declared invoice value at US$ 52,16,272.04, but it made payment upon the tariff value at US$ 13,32,592.00.

24. However, the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs under the signature of the respondent No. 3 has issued the impugned demand letter dated 29-10-2013 stating, inter alia, that—

“০১। সূত্রঃ বি/ই নং-৪৩৩৮, তারিখঃ ২৯-৫-২০১৩ ইং।

উপযুক্ত বিষয়ে আলোকে জানানো যাচ্ছে যে, বি/ই নং-৪৩৩৮, তারিখঃ ২৯-৫-২০১৩ পর্যালোচনা করে দেখা যায় যে, আমদানিকৃত পণ্য চালান CONDENSATE (crude Oil) এর Value তে শুল্কায়ন করা হলেও পণ্য চালানটির Invoice Value Tariff Value এর চেয়ে বেশি হওয়া। The Customs Act, 1969 এর sec-25(3) মোতাবেক Invoice Value ১১২ মাঃ ডলার/ব্যারেল হিসেবে প্রতি কেজি CONDENSATE এর মূল্য ০.৯৩২৪ মাঃ ডলার ধরে শুল্কায়ন করলে পার্থক্য জনিত আদায়যোগ্য শুল্ক-করাদির পরিমাণ দাঁড়ায় ৫,৬২,৬০,৬৭০.৭৩।

২। এমতাবস্থায়, কম আদায়কৃত শুল্ক-করাদি বাবদ ৫,৬২,৬০,৬৭০.৭৩ (পাঁচ কোটি বাষট্টি লক্ষ ষাট হাজার ছয়শত সত্তর দশমিক সাত তিন) টাকা আগামী ১০ (দশ) কার্যদিবসের মধ্যে মংলা কাষ্টমস হাউসের সরকারী কোষাগারে জমা প্রদানের জন্য অনুরোধ করা হলো। অন্যথায়, The Customs Act, 1969 এর sec-202 মোতাবেক আইনানুগ ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করা হবে।”

25. Said impugned demand notice has been challenged by the petitioner on the assertion that without issuing any show cause notice or giving opportunity of being heard, the concerned respondents Customs authority in violation of section 32(3) of the Act has issued the same demanding less payment of customs duty to the tune of Taka 5,62,60,670.73 (five crore sixty two lac sixty thousand six hundred seventy taka and seventy three paisa) on the difference customs duty and taxes between the invoice value and the tariff value.

26. For better understanding the relevant provisions of section 32 of the Act, 1969 is quoted herein below: "32. Untrue statement, error, etc.—(I) If any person, in connection with any matter of customs,—(a) make or signs or causes to made or signed, or delivers or causes to be delivered to an officer of customs any declaration, notice, certificate or other document whatsoever, or (b) makes any statement in answer to any question put to him by an officer of Customs which he is required by or under this Act to answer, [or] (c) transmits any statement, document, information or record through electronic device or produces soft copy thereof, And such document or statement is untrue in any material particular, he shall be guilty of an offence under this section. (2) Where, by reason of any such document or statement as aforesaid or by reason of some collusion, any duty or charge has not been levied or has been short-levied or has been erroneously refunded, the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice, requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice. (3) Where, by reason of any inadvertence, error or misconstruction, any duty or charge [amounting to not less than one thousands taka] has not been levied or has been short-levied or has erroneously refunded the person liable to pay any amount on that account shall be served with a notice, within [three years] of the relevant date, requiring him to show cause why he should not pay the amount specified in the notice. (4) The appropriate officer, after considering the representation, if any, of such person as is referred to in sub-section(2) or sub-section (3) shall determine the amount of duty payable by him which shall in no case exceed the amount specified in the notice, and such person shall pay the amount so determined [Provided that where the amount so determined is less than one thousand take, the person concerned shall not be required to make the payment.] (5) For the purposes of this section, the expression "relevant date" means—(a) in any case where duty is not levied, the duty on which an order for the clearance of goods is made; (b) in a case where duty is provisionally assessed under section 81, the date of adjustment of duty after its final assessment;

(c) in a case where duty has been erroneously refunded, the date of its refund;

(d) in any other case, the date of payment of duty or charge."

27. Section 32 (2) and (3) of the Customs Act, 1969 empowers the Customs authority to demand any customs duty and other charges which has not been levied or shortly levied or erroneously refunded from the person liable to pay the said amount but prior thereto a show cause notice must be served requiring the person concerned to show cause as to why he should not be asked to pay the amount specified in the notice.

28. Sub-section (4) of section 32 provides that the appropriate officer after considering the representation, if any. of such person as is referred to in sub-sections (2) or (3) shall determine the amount of duty payable by him and such person shall pay that amount so determined.

29. It appears from a plain reading of section 32 (2), (3) and (4) of the Act that for determination of actual duty and taxes, which has not been levied or shortly levied or erroneously refunded from the person, the show cause notice must be served. In the present case, the amount of duty has been demanded by the respondent No. 2, the Commissioner of Customs by the impugned demand notice after computing the duty and taxes on the basis of declared invoice value of the petitioner as per provision of section 25(3) of the Act and that said value has not been denied by the petitioner as well as the Customs authority. As such, prior to making demand of the admitted amount does not require issuance of show cause upon the petitioner.

30. Furthermore, Section 202 for the Act empowers the Customs authority to demand any duty to any person, which amount is payable to the government by any person. For ready reference the relevant provision of section 202 is quoted below; 1202.Recovery of Government dues.—(1) When, under this Act, any duty or regulatory duty is payable to the Government by any person or a penalty is adjudged against any person or a notice or demand is served upon any person calling for the payment of any amount unpaid which may be payable by way of duty, regulatory duty, penalty or under any bond, security, guarantee or any other instrument executed under this Act or the rules or orders and such duty, regulatory duty, penalty or other sums due are not paid within the time it was required or ordered to be paid , the appropriate officer may at any time—(a) deduct, or require any other officer of customs to deduct, the amount so payable from any money owing to such person or due which may be in the hands or at the disposal of, or under the control of, the customs authorities or of such officer or of the Government; (b) stop clearance of any goods belonging to such person from customs control in the sea port, airport, any other customs station or from bonded warehouse till such amount is paid or recovered in full;

(c) (d) (e)

(f) (2) (3)

31. It appears from the section 202 of the Act that when any person is liable to pay any duty or regulatory duty to the Government under this Act or a penalty is adjudged against any person or notice or demand is served upon any person calling for the payment of any amount of unpaid duty. regulatory duty,  penalty under this Act or the rules or orders and such duty or other sums due are not paid within the time it was required or ordered to be paid, the Customs officer may at any time take any action as provided under sub-section 1(a) to (f).

32. The impugned demand notice has been issued by the concerned respondent Customs authority with request to deposit Taka 5,62,60,670.73 to the Government treasury within 10 (ten) days, which amount the petitioner is liable to pay under section 25(3) of the Act, failing which action under section 202 of the Act would be taken against it. In view of our above observations and findings, the impugned demand appears to have been issued in due compliance of the provisions of the Customs Act, 1969.

33. Another assertion of the petitioner is that whether the impugned demand notice issued by the concerned respondent Customs authority was in violation of the rules of principle of natural justice i.e. a man shall not be condemned unheard and without having the opportunity of making his defence i.e. audio alteram pertem, since the impugned notice has been issued upon the petitioner without giving opportunity of being heard.

34. What is natural justice, in this question the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Dev Dutt vs Union of India reported in AIR 2008 Supreme Court 2513 paragraph No. 2 observed as under;

"The rules of natural Justice are no codified nor are they unvarying in all situations, rather they are flexible. They may, however, be summarized in one word fairness. In other words, what they require is fairness by the authority concerned. Of course, what is fair would depend on the situation and the context."

35. In Russel vs Duke of Norfolk (1949) All ER 109, 118, the Court held that; "The rules of natural Justice must depend on the circumstances of the case, the natural of the inquiry, the rules under which the authority is acting and the subject matter that is being dealt with."

36. We are in agreement with the above observation that the rules of natural justice depend on the situation, context and circumstances of each case.

37. However, in the instant case, no additional amount of duty or any penalty or fine has been imposed upon the petitioner while issuing the impugned demand. Rather, the actual duty and taxes so assessed earlier was on admitted declared value of the petitioner and that as per proviso to section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 the same has been demanded by the Customs authority giving opportunity to pay the said amount of duty and taxes within 10 (ten) days of receipt of the notice. So, it cannot be said that without giving reasonable time for payment of admitted outstanding duty and taxes, the demand has been made; hence, the impugned demand is very much consonant with Section 202 of the Act, 1969. Moreso, the admitted amount of liability need not be adjudicated by hearing of the party.

38. In the case of SK Akijuddin Ltd. vs National Board of Revenue, reported in 16 BLC 692, the case of Md Musa Bhuiyan vs The Commissioner of Customs, Dhaka reported in 23 BLC 663, and an unreported decision of the case of Jalal Uddin vs National Board of Revenue, in writ petition No 1144 of 2006 (supra), as referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the Customs authority issued the notices demanding to pay additional customs duties and taxes changing the importer's declared HS Code or enhancing invoice value after conducting post clearance audit. While resolving the said dispute this Court has observed inter-alia, that since the demand was not preceded prior to show cause notice as provided under section 32(2)(3) of the Act, 1969 such demand cannot be said to have been made with lawful authority. Even for making any demand under section 83A of the Act, 1969 the principles of natural justice should be applied.

39. In the present case, the notice of demand has been issued on the basis of assessment so made on the declared invoice value of the petitioner, not changing of H.S Code or enhancing the invoice value. Hence, the facts and circumstances of the present case is distinguishable from the cases so referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and hence, not applicable.

40. On perusal of the supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-opposition and the affidavit-in-reply, it appears that the National Board of Revenue on considering the request of Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation as well as the petitioner company had tried to resolve the issue of exemption of additional duty, taxes and VAT on the additional value pertaining to the tariff value following the provision under section 25(3) of the Act, 1969 giving retrospective effect from 9th June 2005. The summary of the said proposal was placed before the Hon'ble Minister, Ministry of Finance for approval and by publishing the notification in the official Gazette. But, before publishing the Gazette, it was sent to the Ministry of Law Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for vetting. However, after vetting the Hon'ble Minister gave opinion, that there was no scope to exempt duty and taxes under the existing law.

<u>41. In view of the said context, the petitioner is liable to pay the admitted unpaid duty and taxes under the Act, 1969 which it cannot avoid to pay on the plea of technicality of law that prior to issuance of the impugned demand, no show cause notice under sections 32 or 83A of the Act, 1969 was served thus, committed violation of the principles of natural justice.</u>

42. Considering the above facts and circumstances of case, observations and findings, we find no substance in the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

43. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to costs.

44. The impugned order dated 29-10-2013 passed under Nothi No. S/4181 /Aa:/ Mongla/12-13/5090(1) by the respondent No. 3 on behalf of the respondent No. 2 (Annexure-F) demanding Taka 5,62,60,670.73 from the petitioner as customs duties and taxes is hereby declared to have been passed with lawful authority.

45. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated and recalled.

46. The petitioner is hereby directed to pay the long outstanding Government revenue to the concerned respondents within a period of 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order; failing which the respondent concern is at liberty to realise the said amount in accordance with law.

Communicate the copy of the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith.

End.
